nurture

/NUR-cher/ - the stress falls on NUR · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Nurture means to care for something and help it develop.

Bakers nurture a sourdough starter for years, feeding it by the clock and guarding it from drafts.

Example

The owlet came to the raptor center as a fist of wet feathers. The staff nurtured her by hand: tweezer-fed at first, then glove-fed; they warmed her box at night, moved her to a flight cage sized to her wingspan, and hid live mice in the straw so that hunting could grow at the pace her wings did.

Nurture is the exact word for that year of care, because nurture means to care for something and help it develop — the feeding and the growing belong together. Protect is only half of it: a protected owl stays alive; a nurtured one learns to hunt.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

raise: Raise means to bring up a child or an animal until it is grown — the word is tied to that job and ends when the growing-up does. Nurture travels wider and needs no finish line: you can nurture a talent, a friendship, or a project, adjusting the care daily so it develops.

look after: To look after something is to keep it safe and fed — the sitter looks after the dog, and success is nothing going wrong. Nurture aims past looking after: nurture points the same care at growth, at helping the thing become more than it was.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

starve: hold back exactly what growth needs

leave untended: give no care and let it fend for itself

Where it sits · how thorough the looking-after becomes

tend → nurture → coddle

tend vs. nurture: Tend is milder than nurture — tending covers the basic chores, water the plant, feed the cat, with no promise of anything more, while nurture aims every feeding at growth.

coddle vs. nurture: Coddle goes further than nurture — nurture builds strength toward independence, while coddling protects so completely that nothing ever toughens.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — nurt: to feed, to nourish (Latin nutrire, via French)

Suffix — -ure: noun-and-verb ending: the act of

Put it together: Nurt (to feed, nourish) + -ure = the act of feeding. Latin nutrire fed everything from infants to orchards, and came into English through French nourriture, 'upbringing.' Nurse and nutrition are its close kin: all three keep food at the center of care.

Use the root in a new word: nutrient: She stood in the cereal aisle comparing the nutrients printed down each box's side panel.

Root Check

Word Choice

warm / hands-on

Nurture is the hands-on member of the caring family: feeding, warming, adjusting, daily. Foster, its unit-mate, arranges conditions from a step back; cherish holds a thing dear without needing it to grow at all. If there is a feeding schedule and the goal is growth, nurture is the word.
